title: Automation: Macros, VBA & Office Scripts
summary: P6 turns the jobs you repeat every day into one click: record macros, then write VBA that loops, decides, asks and checks, and builds real reports, PDFs and emails, safely. It ends with Office Scripts for Excel on the web.
prereq: Builds on C1 · Excel Foundations and C2 · Formulas & Functions. No coding background is needed: every line of VBA is explained from the start.
outcomes: Decide what is worth automating, and keep macro workbooks safe: file types, the Trust Center, blocked files and trusted locations.
Record macros with absolute and relative references, run them from buttons and shortcuts, and clean up the recorder’s code.
Find your way round the Visual Basic Editor and Excel’s objects: workbooks, sheets, ranges, properties and methods.
Write VBA with variables, decisions, loops and arrays that work on however many rows the data has.
Talk to users with message boxes, input boxes, UserForms and events, and stop bad input before it lands.
Debug with breakpoints, stepping and the Immediate window, handle errors, and make slow macros fast.
Automate real reports: format, split, merge files from a folder, save PDFs and prepare emails.
Write your own worksheet functions, and automate Excel for the web with Office Scripts and Power Automate.

lessons.title: Finding bugs
lessons.summary: A bug is code that runs but does the wrong thing, or stops with an error. Don’t guess: stop the macro where it goes wrong with a breakpoint or F8, read the values in Locals and the Immediate window, and you’ll see which line and which value are wrong. Debug.Print leaves a trail; Stop and Debug.Assert stop when something unexpected happens.
objectives: Step through a macro with F8, Shift+F8 and Run to Cursor, and stop it at breakpoints.
Read values while it’s stopped: Locals, hovering, and ? in the Immediate window.
Fix the common bugs: the wrong column for the last row, overflowing types, off-by-one loops.

topics: Leave a trail, stop on surprises

lessons.title: Handling run-time errors
lessons.summary: Some errors aren’t bugs: a sheet someone deleted, a file that isn’t there, packs typed in words. On Error GoTo sends the macro to a handler instead of the grey error box; Err says what went wrong; Resume Next carries on after the line that failed. On Error Resume Next skips one risky line, if you check Err straight after.
objectives: Catch run-time errors with On Error GoTo and a handler label, with Exit Sub before it.
Tell the user what went wrong with Err.Number and Err.Description.
Carry on after a bad row with Resume Next, or retry with Resume.
Test something risky with On Error Resume Next, check Err, and switch back with On Error GoTo 0.
topics: The grey box isn’t for users

lessons.title: Clean exits and your own errors
lessons.summary: A macro that turns off screen updating, events or automatic calculation must turn them back on however it ends, error or not. One CleanUp label that every route goes through does it. Log what went wrong for later, and raise your own errors, with Err.Raise, when your code finds something it can’t carry on with.
objectives: Put settings back on every way out with a CleanUp label and Resume CleanUp.
Log errors to a sheet with the time, the macro and Err.Number and Err.Description.

lessons.title: Office Scripts
lessons.summary: Excel for the web can’t run VBA. Office Scripts do the same kind of job there: small programs in TypeScript, started from the Automate tab, that read and change the workbook. Everything begins with main(workbook); ranges have get and set methods; getValues and setValues move a whole block at once.

lessons.title: Power Automate: scripts that run themselves
lessons.summary: Power Automate runs your Office Scripts without anyone opening Excel: at six every evening, when a file arrives, or from a button. A flow passes values into main through its parameters and gets back whatever main returns, which the next step can put in an email or a Teams message.
objectives: Describe a flow: a trigger, then actions, including Excel’s Run script.
Give main a parameter and a return type, so a flow can pass data in and get an answer back.
Write a script that’s safe in a flow: named sheets, no selection, no outside calls.
Choose between VBA, Office Scripts and a flow for a job.

lessons.title: Handing over your tools
lessons.summary: A macro only helps the team if someone else can run it, change it and trust it after you’ve moved on. Option Explicit and good names catch mistakes early; settings on a sheet let people change rates and folders without touching code; a locked project and a digital signature protect it; and a Readme sheet and a code backup make the handover real.
objectives: Use Option Explicit and declared variables so typos are caught before a macro runs.
Move numbers and paths the team changes onto a Settings sheet and read them in code.
Lock a VBA project and sign it with a digital certificate, and know what each does.
Write a header comment, a Readme sheet and a code backup for handover.
topics: Settings on a sheet, not in the code
